threads.name: Local Docker startup is too slow

root.author: ziad
root.text: Cold `docker compose up` from scratch takes ~7 minutes on my machine before I can even hit the app. Is everyone living with this or am I doing it wrong?

replies.author: salma
replies.text: A lot of that is the seed + migrations running on every boot. If you already have a DB volume you can skip reseeding with `SEED=skip`.

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: The other chunk is images being rebuilt. Are you on `make bootstrap` (pulls prebuilt) or `docker compose build` (builds locally)? The latter is way slower.

replies.author: ziad
replies.text: ...I was running `docker compose build` every time 🙈

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: There it is. Pull the prebuilt images and only build the service you're actually changing. Should drop you to ~90s.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: We should honestly make the slow path harder to hit by accident. Rename the build target so nobody runs it out of habit.

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: Fair. I'll split it into `make dev` (fast, prebuilt) and `make build-local` (explicit). Updating the README too.

replies.author: ziad
replies.text: 90s now. night and day, thank you both 🙏

threads.name: Should we adopt a shared devcontainer?

root.author: youssef
root.text: Proposal: ship a devcontainer config so onboarding is 'open in container' instead of a 20-step README. New hires burned a full day last time. Thoughts?

replies.author: omar
replies.text: In favor if it doesn't fork our workflow — I don't want to maintain both a devcontainer and native setup forever.

replies.author: ahmed
replies.text: Frontend folks mostly run node natively for speed. A container that mounts the repo is fine but full-in-container hot reload has been painful for me historically.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: Backend it'd help a lot — the pain is always postgres/redis versions drifting from prod. Container pins those.

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: What if the container is the default 'just works' path, but native stays documented and supported for people who want raw speed? Not either/or.

replies.author: reem
replies.text: From onboarding side, anything that gets a new engineer to a running app on day one is a huge win. Ziad's first week was mostly environment yak-shaving.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Ok, green light for the container as the default onboarding path, native stays first-class. Keep it thin.

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: On it. Will target getting Ziad's replacement... I mean the next hire... to a running app in under an hour 😄

threads.name: CI got slow again during crunch

root.author: karim
root.text: Backend CI crept back up to 15 min this week. I think we're re-running the heavy seed inside integration tests now that large-channel perf work landed. Can we look before this becomes the norm?

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: Yeah the perf tests pull the heavy seed. Problem is they run in the same job as the fast unit tests so everyone pays for it.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: Split them. Fast unit + lightweight integration on every PR, heavy perf tests as a separate opt-in job + nightly.

replies.author: mariam
replies.text: As long as the perf tests still run before we tag a release I'm fine with them not being on every PR.

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: Done — perf tests are their own job now, gated to the perf label + nightly + release branch. PR CI back to 9 min.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: 9 min, confirmed on my last PR. Thanks for jumping on it mid-crunch 🙏

replies.author: omar
replies.text: This is exactly the 'make it loud here' I asked for. Good catch @karim.

root.author: mariam
root.text: The calendar-sync integration tests are flaky — duplicate webhook events sometimes arrive out of order in the test and the assertion count is off. Real bug or test setup?

replies.author: karim
replies.text: That's actually the real idempotency work — the test is exposing that we weren't deduping webhook events reliably. Not just a flaky test.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: Right, we're adding idempotency keys so a duplicate webhook is a no-op. The test should assert on final state, not on how many events were processed.

replies.author: mariam
replies.text: Ah that makes sense. I'll rewrite the assertion to check the resulting calendar state instead of the event count.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: And once idempotency keys are in, the retries won't create duplicates either, so the flakiness disappears at the source.

replies.author: mariam
replies.text: Rewrote it + retested against the idempotency branch, 10/10 green. Much better signal now.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: nice, that's one fewer thing masking real regressions 🎉

root.author: omar
root.text: Design question for thread notifications before we build: do we auto-subscribe you to a thread when you reply, when you're @mentioned, or both? This decision shapes the whole data model.

replies.author: lina
replies.text: Both, but with an easy escape hatch. If I reply I clearly care; if I'm mentioned someone wants me. The escape hatch is a per-thread mute.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: From the backend side, both is fine as long as we store an explicit subscription row per (user, thread) with a state — subscribed / muted / none. No implicit magic.

replies.author: daniel
replies.text: Please make the states explicit, yes. If it's implicit I can't build a meaningful "why did I get this notification" audit later, and support tickets about phantom pings will be miserable.

replies.author: hana
replies.text: UX-wise I want a visible indicator on the thread showing you're subscribed, plus a one-tap mute. If people can't see or control it, notifications feel like spam and they turn everything off.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Okay, converging: explicit subscription row, three states, auto-subscribe on reply or mention, one-tap mute with a visible indicator. Karim I'll write the schema, you take the delivery path?

replies.author: karim
replies.text: Deal. I'll have the delivery + fan-out design in the doc by Thursday.

root.author: lina
root.text: Kicking off guest access planning for 3.0 since Adam and Sara keep (rightly) pushing. Core question: is a guest a limited seat, or a fundamentally different entity? This affects billing, permissions, and SSO.

replies.author: adam
replies.text: From a sales angle it has to be free or near-free to the customer, otherwise it's just a seat and there's no reason to call it a guest. NovaTech wants to add contractors without growing their bill.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Technically the cleanest is a limited seat with a restricted role — same user entity, scoped permissions. A separate entity means duplicating half our auth logic. Please let's not.

replies.author: sara
replies.text: Whatever the model, the guest experience has to be obviously restricted so customers trust it. My accounts worry a contractor will stumble into channels they shouldn't see. Channel-scoped by default is the ask.

replies.author: maya
replies.text: Constraints I care about: near-zero cost to the customer, channel-scoped access, and it must not blow up our SSO story for 3.0. If those three hold, I'm flexible on implementation.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Limited seat + restricted role + channel-scoped invites satisfies all three and reuses our auth. I'll write it up that way. Billing treats guests as non-charged seats with a cap per workspace.

replies.author: lina
replies.text: Great, that's our direction. I'll draft the 3.0 spec around it and we revisit after 2.9 ships. Thanks all 🙏

threads.name: Defining an activity metric for DAU

root.author: daniel
root.text: We need to nail down what counts as "active" for DAU before Analytics V2 ships. Right now I count any authenticated session. But a user who just has the app open in a background tab and never does anything is inflating the number. Proposals?

replies.author: lina
replies.text: I'd argue active = performed a meaningful action: sent a message, completed a task, reacted, joined a call. Opening a tab shouldn't count.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Agree with meaningful action. Presence heartbeats alone are too noisy, and it makes us look better than we are which helps no one.

replies.author: daniel
replies.text: OK so the definition is: sent message OR task action OR reaction OR joined meeting OR posted in thread, within the day, in the workspace's timezone. That'll drop our DAU maybe 12-15% but it's honest.

replies.author: maya
replies.text: Honest number every time. I'd rather quote 440 real actives than 510 fluffy ones on a sales call. Do it.

replies.author: lina
replies.text: Can we keep the old "session" number as a secondary metric so we don't lose the trend line history?

replies.author: daniel
replies.text: Yep, I'll keep both columns. "Active" (meaningful action) as primary, "Sessions" as secondary. Backfilling the last 90 days now so the trend is consistent.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Nice. Document the definition in the metrics readme so we don't relitigate this in three months 😄

root.author: daniel
root.text: Investigating a sharp DAU drop last Friday, ~18% down day over day with no obvious cause. Not a holiday. Anyone deploy anything Thursday night?

threads.name: Calendar sync duplicate events — root cause

root.author: salma
root.text: Digging into the duplicate calendar events. It's not just the double webhook — even after dedupe I'm seeing occasional dupes on retry. Sharing what I've found so far.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: So there are two sources: (1) Google delivering the same push twice, and (2) our own retry firing after a slow-but-successful write. The second one is on us.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: Right. For (1) an idempotency key on the resource+eventId dedupes cleanly. For (2) we need the write and the 'processed' marker in the same transaction so a retry sees it as done.

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: The retry is coming from the queue's visibility timeout being shorter than a slow sync. I can bump the timeout, but the transactional marker is the real fix.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: Let's do both: idempotency key keyed on (channel, provider_event_id) with a unique constraint, plus mark-processed inside the same tx. Belt and suspenders.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: Writing it up. Unique constraint will make the dupe insert a no-op at the DB level, which is the safety net I wanted.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: This is the pattern I want everywhere we touch external webhooks. Salma can you note it in the eng wiki once it lands?

threads.name: Audit log export format: CSV vs API

root.author: adam
root.text: Enterprise customers keep asking how they get audit logs OUT. BetaWorks wants SIEM ingestion. What are we offering — CSV download, streaming API, or both?

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Both, but different priorities. CSV export for humans/compliance folks. A paginated JSON API for SIEM/automation. Streaming/webhook can come later.

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: For SIEM the important part is a stable cursor so they can pull incrementally without gaps or dupes. Idempotent, ordered by event time + a monotonic id.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: I'll make the API cursor-based on a monotonic sequence rather than timestamp alone — timestamps collide under load and you'd miss events.

replies.author: mariam
replies.text: I'll test the incremental pull specifically: pull, insert new events, pull again with the cursor, assert no overlap and no missing rows.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Perfect. CSV for the 2.9 beta, JSON pull API right after. Webhook streaming is a fast-follow if a customer actually needs push.

replies.author: adam
replies.text: That's more than enough to unblock BetaWorks. Their IT confirmed pull-based is fine for their SIEM.

root.author: omar
root.text: Question that keeps coming up: SSO handles authentication, but do we need SCIM for automated user provisioning/deprovisioning in 2.9? Especially deprovisioning matters for security.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: JIT provisioning covers creation on first login. The real gap is deprovisioning — if someone leaves the customer's org, SAML alone won't disable their PulseDesk account.

replies.author: adam

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: Short-term answer: admin can bulk-deactivate, and a SAML login failure after the user is removed from the IdP means they can't get back in. Full SCIM is a bigger project.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Right. For 2.9 we document: SSO gates access so removing them from the IdP blocks login immediately, plus admin deactivation. SCIM goes on the post-2.9 roadmap.

replies.text: That's a defensible position for now. But let's put SCIM on the enterprise roadmap explicitly — it'll be a hard requirement the moment we chase a customer over ~500 seats.

root.author: sara
root.text: Digging into the NovaTech calendar duplicates more. Their admin says ~6 users saw the same meeting appear 2-3 times after they connected Google Calendar. Not everyone, and only on recurring events. Anyone seen this pattern?

replies.author: salma
replies.text: Recurring events lining up with it makes sense. The provider fires a webhook per instance and if a retry comes in before we ack, we process it twice. No idempotency key currently means we insert twice.

replies.author: sara
replies.text: So it's specifically recurring + a retry racing the ack? That explains why it's only some users.

replies.author: salma

root.text: Idempotency keys handle duplicates, but we still have the other half of calendar sync: failed webhook deliveries. Right now if our handler 500s, the event is just lost. We need retries with backoff. Opening this up for design.

replies.author: youssef

replies.author: karim
replies.text: Queue. Push the raw event to a durable queue immediately on receipt, ack the webhook fast, then process async with retries. Provider stops retrying because we 200 quickly.

replies.author: salma

replies.text: 5 retries, exponential backoff, then dead-letter queue with an alert. We can replay from the DLQ manually once fixed.

replies.text: This is the right shape. Combined with idempotency keys, reprocessing a DLQ event is safe because dupes get dropped. Ship it.

root.author: omar
root.text: Thread notifications design thread. The hard part: when someone replies in a thread, we notify everyone who participated in that thread OR is following it, deduped, respecting mute settings, across potentially large threads. Karim, walk us through the plan.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: On reply, we resolve the participant set: thread authors + explicit followers, minus muters, minus the replier. Then batch-insert notifications and fan out to the delivery workers. The old code did this synchronously in the request path, which is why it choked.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: How big can a thread participant set realistically get? If it's a 500-reply thread in a big channel that's a lot of fan-out per reply.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: That's why it moves off the request path entirely. Reply request just enqueues a fan-out job and returns. Worker pool handles the expansion and delivery.

replies.author: ziad
replies.text: Do we collapse rapid replies? If someone posts 5 times in 10 seconds I don't want 5 pings.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Good point. Debounce per-thread-per-recipient with a short window, say 30s, then send a single notification. Lina asked for exactly this actually.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: I'll add the debounce in the worker using a Redis key per (thread, recipient). Cheap and self-expiring.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: Make sure the mute check happens at delivery time, not enqueue time. Someone might mute the thread between the reply and delivery.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: Yep, delivery-time mute check. Enqueue is cheap and possibly-stale, delivery is authoritative. Writing it up in the PR.

root.author: omar
root.text: We keep hitting the same class of bug: duplicate processing of events. Calendar webhooks, thread notifications, probably others. Rather than fix each one-off, I want to align on a shared idempotency pattern. Proposals?

replies.author: karim
replies.text: For calendar I went with a Redis-backed dedup key on (provider, event_id, resource_state), 72h TTL. It's simple and works. I'd propose we standardize on that shape: a dedup key derived from stable event attributes, stored with a TTL longer than the max upstream retry window.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: Redis is fine for high-volume ephemeral dedup, but for things that must never double-process even after Redis eviction (payments, audit events) we need a durable store. Postgres unique constraint on the idempotency key. Two tiers depending on criticality.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: I like the two-tier framing. Ephemeral/high-volume → Redis TTL, must-never-duplicate → Postgres unique constraint. Let's document both and pick per use case.

replies.author: daniel
replies.text: For the analytics pipeline I dedup at the consumer with the Kafka offset + event id. Slightly different because it's a stream, but same principle. Should I fold that into the shared doc or keep it separate?

replies.author: karim
replies.text: Fold it in as the 'stream consumer' variant. Three patterns, one doc, one decision guide. I'll write the first draft.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: One more thing to call out in the doc: idempotency keys are worthless if the operation isn't actually idempotent downstream. Dedup at the boundary AND make the handler safe to retry. Belt and suspenders.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Yes. That's the real lesson. Karim, draft it, tag me and salma for review, and let's make it required reading. This has cost us enough bugs.

root.text: Design question on guest access: how do we handle guest session expiry? Options: (a) hard expiry, guest is logged out at N days and must be re-invited, (b) sliding window, activity extends it, (c) admin-configurable. Leaning (a) for security but want input.

replies.author: lina
replies.text: From a product angle, hard expiry with re-invite is annoying if a guest is actively collaborating on a project that runs 3 weeks. But sliding windows can leave guests with access forever, which is exactly what enterprise security teams hate.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: Security take: default to hard expiry, but make the duration admin-configurable with a sane default (say 14 days). That satisfies the security-conscious admins and the collaborative use case, without us guessing.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Agree with salma. (a) + (c) combined. Hard expiry, admin sets the window, default 14 days. No sliding window — it's an audit nightmare to explain 'this guest still has access because they clicked something 2 months ago.'

replies.author: hana
replies.text: UX-wise we should warn the guest and the host before expiry, not just cut access. A 'this guest's access expires in 2 days, extend?' prompt for the host. Silent lockout feels broken even when it's intended.

replies.author: lina
replies.text: Yes, the pre-expiry warning to the host is the key detail that makes hard expiry feel intentional instead of buggy. Good call hana.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: Settled then: hard expiry, admin-configurable window, 14-day default, host warning at T-2 days. Ziad, this affects your permission checks, want to pair on the expiry logic?

root.author: karim
root.text: Let's lock the idempotency design before we build more on top of it. Proposal: dedupe key = sha256(provider + resourceId + messageNumber) for Google, sha256(provider + subscriptionId + resourceData.id + changeType) for MS. Store in a unique index, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING at insert. Thoughts?

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: Where do you want the dedupe to happen, at the queue consumer or the DB? If it's DB-level unique index we get it for free even across instances.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: DB-level. That's the whole point, it survives races between pods. The consumer just tries the insert and moves on if it conflicts.

replies.author: mariam

replies.author: salma
replies.text: Yes, I'll emit a webhook.deduped metric with provider label. You can assert on the counter delta.

replies.author: karim

threads.name: Retry backoff tuning after the weekend incident

root.author: youssef
root.text: Post-mortem on Saturday's retry storm. Ingestion endpoint returned 503 for 6 minutes during a node drain, Google queued and re-sent aggressively. We ack'd late so it counted as failures. Queue hit 12k. We recovered but I want to prevent it structurally.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: The core fix is what we discussed weeks ago but never fully did: return 200 the instant we persist the raw payload, before any processing. Provider sees success, no retry storm.

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: Right. During the drain we were processing synchronously inside the request. I'll make the drain also cordon the ingestion service so it stops receiving before it goes unhealthy.

replies.author: salma
replies.text: I can split it: a thin receiver that only writes raw payload + returns 200, and a worker that processes from the queue. That decouples provider-facing availability from our processing health.

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: That's exactly the shape I want. Then even a full worker outage just grows the queue, it never triggers retries.

replies.author: mariam
replies.text: How do I test that the receiver stays up when the worker is down? Can we have a chaos toggle?

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: I'll add a staging switch to kill the worker while keeping the receiver alive. You should see 200s continuing and queue depth climbing, then a clean drain when the worker comes back.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: Let's target this for before the 2.9 freeze. It's the last big structural risk in the pipeline.

root.author: lina
root.text: Decision thread: do we ship guest access in 2.9 or defer to 2.9.1? Need a call by end of week so QA can plan. Please weigh in with real status, not optimism 🙂

replies.author: karim
replies.text: Backend: permission model + scoped tokens are done and tested. What's NOT done is the invite flow and the billing hook (guests shouldn't count as billable seats). That's ~1.5 weeks of work I don't have before freeze.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: The billing tie-in is the scary part. If we get guest seat counting wrong customers get overcharged and that's a support/trust nightmare. I'd rather ship it right in 2.9.1.

replies.author: hana
replies.text: Design for the invite-as-guest flow is only ~70% done anyway. I'd welcome the extra cycle to get the permission-scoping UI clear.

replies.author: mariam
replies.text: From QA: I have zero test coverage on guest access and it touches billing + permissions, the two areas I'd want most time on. Deferring makes my regression pass for 2.9 much safer.

replies.author: lina
replies.text: That's unanimous enough for me. Decision: guest access is DEFERRED to 2.9.1. Flag stays off in the 2.9 build. Karim's backend work stays merged behind the flag so we're not throwing it away. Thanks all.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Agreed. Good, clean call. Let's put guest access at the top of the 2.9.1 scope so it doesn't drift.

threads.name: Large-channel perf — is it a ship blocker?

root.author: mariam
root.text: Raising this properly since it's borderline. On a mid-tier Android, a 2,000-message channel renders in 3.1s and scroll gets janky past ~800 messages. Our budget is 2s. Blocker for 2.9 or not?

replies.author: ahmed
replies.text: Root cause is we render the whole message list into the DOM. Windowed rendering (only render what's visible + a buffer) would fix both the render time and the scroll jank. I have a prototype idea, ~3-4 days.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: NovaTech has channels with 50k+ messages. If we ship 2.9 with visible jank on big channels they'll feel it day one and it undercuts the whole 'faster' story. I lean toward making it a blocker IF we can land it before freeze.

replies.author: karim
replies.text: Backend can help — I can add cursor-based pagination on the message history endpoint so the client isn't even fetching 2,000 at once. Complements the windowing nicely.

replies.author: ahmed
replies.text: Cursor pagination + windowing together would be ideal. Let me spike the windowing tomorrow and I'll report numbers before we commit to calling it a blocker.

replies.author: mariam
replies.text: Works for me. I'll hold PD-2958 as 'pending perf spike' and we decide blocker status once Ahmed has real numbers.

replies.author: ahmed
replies.text: Update: prototype done, 2,000-message channel now 1.2s and smooth. Numbers are good enough that I think we should just land it rather than defer. Putting up the PR.

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Beautiful. Land it before freeze and it's in. Nice work — this is the difference between a good release and a great one.

root.author: youssef
root.text: Locking the rollout plan for the 21st. Proposal: canary to 5% of workspaces, hold 2h watching error rate + p95 + notification queue depth, then 25%, then 100% over ~24h. Automated rollback if error rate > 2x baseline for 5min. Objections?

replies.author: omar
replies.text: Solid. Add task-completion event ingestion to the watch list — Daniel's analytics depend on it and a silent drop there wouldn't show in error rates.

replies.author: daniel
replies.text: +1. I'll wire an ingestion-lag alert so if events stop flowing on the canary cohort we know within a minute, not at the next QBR 😅

replies.author: karim
replies.text: Please also watch the notification fan-out p95 specifically. It's new in 2.9 and it's the thing most likely to misbehave under real load.

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: Added: task-event ingestion lag + fan-out p95 to the canary dashboard. Rollback stays one command and I've rehearsed it on staging twice.

replies.author: mariam
replies.text: Can we also keep the canary cohort off our biggest customers for the first ramp? I'd rather NovaTech not be in the 5%.

replies.author: youssef
replies.text: Good call — canary cohort will exclude the top 20 accounts until we hit 100%. Updated the cohort selector. I think we're ready.

root.author: lina
root.text: For onboarding v2 to count as a win we need to prove it moves activation. Daniel, can we instrument the three checklist steps so we can compare first-week activation vs the old flow?

replies.author: daniel
replies.text: Yes. I'll emit an event per checklist step (channel created / teammate invited / first task) plus a 'checklist completed' event. Then activation = % of new workspaces completing all three in 7 days. We can A/B old vs new if you want.

replies.author: lina
replies.text: A/B would be ideal but I don't want to slow the ship. Can we do old-vs-new as a before/after comparison instead, since old-flow data already exists?

replies.author: daniel
replies.text: Before/after works given we have historical funnel data. Caveat: seasonality and the fact 2.9 changes other things too, so I'll caveat the readout as directional, not causal.

replies.author: hana
replies.text: Can we also capture where people drop off in the checklist? If everyone stalls on 'invite a teammate' that's a design signal for 2.9.1.

replies.author: daniel
replies.text: Already in — per-step completion + drop-off is part of the same instrumentation. I'll build a small funnel view in the analytics dashboard so it's self-serve.

replies.author: lina
replies.text: Perfect. This is exactly what I want to show Sara for the BetaWorks renewal conversation. Thanks Daniel 🙏
